etymology: Of multiple origins, partly from French liberal and partly from Latin līberālis, “befitting a free man,” per the Oxford English Dictionary, which records its earliest evidence from around 1384, in the Wycliffite Bible. The OED lists political senses from the late 1700s. The older, scriptural sense, open-handed and generous, has its own entry: see liberal.
biblical_def: In politics, liberal has meant two nearly opposite things. The older political liberalism, now called classical liberalism, stood for civil liberties under the rule of law, limited government, free markets and freedom of speech; until the Great Depression it was simply called economic liberalism. Modern liberalism in the United States emerged with Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal in the 1930s. In 1941 Roosevelt defined the liberal party as the one that believes that, as new problems arise beyond the power of men and women to meet as individuals, “it becomes the duty of Government itself to find new remedies.” Today in the United States the bare term usually means social or progressive liberalism, associated with the center-left. The Christian observation: the King James Bible uses liberal in its root sense of free-handed generosity. “The liberal soul shall be made fat: and he that watereth shall be watered also himself” (Pro 11:25), and “the liberal deviseth liberal things; and by liberal things shall he stand” (Isa 32:8).
webster_summary: In politics, first a creed of limited government and civil liberty (classical liberalism), then, from the New Deal of the 1930s, a creed of expanded government action (modern American liberalism). From Latin līberālis, befitting a free man (OED about 1384). Scripture’s liberal is the generous man (Pro 11:25).
webster_full: LIBERAL, adj. and n. (political senses from the late 1700s, OED) 1. Favouring individual liberty, limited government and free markets (now usually classical liberal). 2. In modern U.S. usage, favouring government action for social and economic ends; centre-left. From French liberal and Latin līberālis.

History note: modern liberalism in the United States emerged with the New Deal in the 1930s; the earlier sense was renamed classical liberalism as a retronym (Wikipedia, “Modern liberalism in the United States”; “Classical liberalism”).

corruption_summary: Liberal meant generous, then free; in American politics the name was kept while the view of government’s role reversed, so the same word now usually stands for the expansion of government that the older liberal resisted.
corruption_paragraphs: The word has travelled a long way from its root. Līberālis described what befits a free man, and the King James translators used liberal for the open hand that gives of its own (Pro 11:25). Classical liberalism carried the idea of freedom into politics as limited government. Modern American liberalism, from the New Deal on, kept the name and reversed much of the content, so that the same word now usually means the expansion of government into matters the older liberal kept from it.

Scripture’s own use of the word is a man’s free-handed giving of what is his, devised by a liberal heart (Isa 32:8; Pro 11:25). Its teaching on liberty is that freedom is not licence: “use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another” (Gal 5:13). A word that has meant both limited government and expanded government cannot settle any argument by itself; the Christian should ask which meaning is in use and weigh the policy, not the label, by the word of God.
roots_summary: Latin līberālis, befitting a free man → liberal, generous (OED about 1384; KJV) → political sense (late 1700s), limited government → New Deal liberalism (1930s), expanded government.
roots_lines: About 1384: OED’s earliest evidence for liberal, Wycliffite Bible
1930s: modern American liberalism emerges with the New Deal; the older creed is renamed classical liberalism (Wikipedia)
usage: “The nineteenth-century liberal wanted less government; his namesake today usually wants more.”
